evals.prompt: Our PRs take forever to get merged and everyone blames CI. Can you make an interactive diagram of our pipeline for the team wiki? We push maybe 30 PRs a day, CI takes about 8 minutes, two of us review (most reviews are 15-20 minutes but some take an hour), and about 1 in 5 PRs gets changes requested. Single HTML file is fine.
evals.expected_output: A standalone HTML page with one figure built from a model.mjs: lanes for author, CI and review, CI as a station (possibly with an inside showing its jobs), review with servers matching the stated people and a logn work time with the stated median and p95, a rework loop back to the author through the same queue. The model is calibrated on several seeds (utilization at the bottleneck reported), the caption is generated from the run and states where the time actually goes with measured numbers, claims for every number in the prose, `--audit` passes, and the what-if the caption names (one more reviewer, or similar) is one click away and was checked in headless Chrome. No number in the caption or prose was typed by hand.

evals.prompt: I'm writing a blog post on why caches matter. Make me an interactive figure of a request going from the browser through a CDN, a load balancer, an app server, Redis and Postgres. I want readers to be able to see what happens when the cache hit rate drops.
evals.expected_output: A figure whose items travel with real latencies across the network lanes, with the app server as a station with an inside (Redis lookup, a hit-or-miss choice by chance, Postgres with limited capacity). The base run and the cold-cache what-if are both measured; the numbers are tuned so the what-if produces a visible effect (workers filling, a queue, timeouts) and the caption reports what was measured, not what was hoped for. The choice offers the 'miss twice as often' what-if. Audit passes; captures at 1280 and 390 px, light and dark, were read.

evals.prompt: explain how TCP retransmission works with something visual and interactive, I always forget the difference between fast retransmit and an RTO
evals.expected_output: An interactive figure in which items are segments: the sender's and receiver's stacks (optionally with their layers as lanes inside), a router with a finite buffer whose overflow drops segments (capacity, outcome rejected), and the two recovery paths after a drop as timers of the right lengths (about one round trip for three duplicate ACKs, 200 ms or more for the retransmission timer). Units in ms, a pace set so a round trip is visible, a caption generated from the run that contrasts what each path costs. The figure's simplifications (no congestion control, if left out) are stated in the model comment and the prose.

evals.prompt: Necesito una visualización interactiva de cómo funciona una arquitectura pub/sub para una charla: un servicio de pedidos publica un evento y lo consumen email, inventario y analítica. Quiero mostrar que si email se cae los demás siguen funcionando.
evals.expected_output: A figure (labels and prose may be in Spanish or English as the user prefers; the skill's rules still apply) with a fan-out split (fanout: true) from the topic to one lane per subscriber, each with its own station (consumers as servers), queue and end; email with failures, a retry timer with a cap and a dead-letter end marked seldom. The outage what-if on the email consumer was driven in headless Chrome and the other subscribers' queues were checked to stay unaffected. Caption numbers generated per subscriber from the log.

evals.prompt: We're moving our checkout to Lambda. Build a React component for our Next.js docs that shows a request through API Gateway into a Lambda with reserved concurrency 10, cold starts, and then an SQS queue feeding a fulfillment Lambda. I want to show why the queue matters during traffic spikes.
evals.expected_output: A model plus a Next.js integration: the figure HTML built at build time with buildFigure and the CSS from css(), and a small client component that calls boot() once mounted (as in references/kit.md), plus a standalone HTML preview. The model has a station with servers 10 and capacity 0 (refusing with 429), a cold-start branch by chance inside the function, a fan-out that answers the client and enqueues, and a fulfillment station with its own capacity and retries. The burst what-if was measured (refusals on the sync path, the queue growing and draining on the async path) and the caption reports it.

evals.prompt: Can you make something that shows how computer memory works, all the way from flip-flops and bits up to the full cache hierarchy and RAM? Interactive if possible, for a computer architecture class.
evals.expected_output: A deeply nested figure in nanoseconds: the top level a load through the load ports and L1 with a hit-or-miss choice, a miss path through L2, L3 and DRAM, and levels that open down to the circuit (an SRAM array read ending in a flip-flop latch, DRAM row activation where a bit is a capacitor). Per-level time scales so picosecond steps are visible when opened and nanosecond trips are watchable on top. Realistic timings and hit rates stated as assumptions. Caption generated from the run (the share of time spent on the rare DRAM trips).

evals.prompt: Our on-call rotation is burning people out. I'd like a figure for an internal post that shows how alerts flow from monitoring to the on-call engineer, escalation to the secondary after 15 minutes, and then to the owning team or an incident war room. Most of our alerts are noise.
evals.expected_output: A human-process figure in minutes: alerts with classes (noise and real) and their colors, one on-call station with patience 15 and an escalation route on timeout, class-based routes to false alarm and to the team, a war room as a station whose inside runs mitigation and the status page in parallel. Calibrated on a noisy shift with a representative seed; the 'Half the noise' what-if is available on the start, measured in the caption, and checked in the browser.

evals.prompt: make a simple animated flowchart of our support ticket process: ticket comes in, tier 1 handles it, if they can't solve it it goes to tier 2, then it's closed. nothing fancy, just for a slide
evals.expected_output: Even for a 'simple' request, a real model rather than a flowchart that moves: a Figure-sized level (start, tier 1 and tier 2 as stations with servers and logn work times, a choice or outcome routes for escalation, an end), plausible numbers stated as assumptions and offered for the user to replace, a generated caption with one measured lesson (where tickets wait), audit passing, a standalone page, built in well under an hour without asking for permission to start.

evals.prompt: How does a site actually survive a DDoS? I want an interactive figure for a talk: a Cloudflare-style edge (WAF, rate limiting, a challenge, the CDN cache), then a load balancer, autoscaled app servers and a database. I want to switch each layer on and off, change the size of the attack and the autoscaling limit, and see when the site falls over.
evals.expected_output: A figure that starts from the design that works and lets the reader take it apart: kinds of items (people's requests and bots, ideally pages that need the origin apart from cacheable assets) with their own odds at every layer (fail and p by kind), a switch on each defense layer (a bypass route on the cache), dials on the attack's start (with a none option that pauses it) and on the autoscaling (scale with min, max, target, every and boot), whose settings open on the figure next to their parts rather than in a panel of their own, a database that does not scale, a dot that stands for many requests (per) so the page stays light (no heavy-run warning), figure.watch on the share of pages served, a caption generated from the run and from variants with layers off (what each layer stops, what happens while new servers boot), claims checked on eight seeds, timeout routes marked seldom, --audit --check passing, and a drive that turns a layer off and sees the readout fall.

evals.prompt: I run load tests with k6 against a small Node API, and the metrics go to InfluxDB and Grafana. Make an interactive figure of one run, request by request, for the project's README: the virtual users ramping up, the API's event loop, k6's checks and thresholds, and the samples on their way to the dashboards. Let me point it at my own API instead, and turn the metrics output off.
evals.expected_output: A figure whose load is a closed start (vus stages and think, as the scenario sets them, with its routes as classes) rather than an arrival rate, the API's single event loop as one station with work by kind (a CPU-heavy route holding it while the others wait), a timer for any route that waits without holding the loop, k6's check as a choice (when ok, a late:<time> route for answers past its deadline, else to failed) with an emit route for the samples (dashed, of their own kind) to a metrics path with its own pacing (the output's flush, the dashboards' refresh), a target choice whose dial picks the toy API or the user's own (take, restart, a change of classes) with the user's API as a station whose dials set its answer time and how many it takes at once, a switch on the metrics output, figure.watch over the request kinds only with the p95, a caption generated from the run and variants (a slower route, the user's API under more users than it takes) stating the p95, the failed share and k6's exit code against the thresholds, every number taken from the repository or marked measured or assumed, --audit --check passing.

evals.prompt: /dissect the fundamental flows of this project as interactive figures
evals.expected_output: The agent reads the repository before anything else (entry points, the steps work goes through, queues and workers and their concurrency, timeouts, retries and backoff, the odds the code sets), then names the two or three flows a newcomer needs and says why, and builds one figure each, the most central first, sized as a Figure or a Hero. Every number in a model is taken from the code or its config with the file named in the model's comments, measured where the agent can run something, or an assumption it states in the comments and in the prose. Each figure has abouts on the steps a reader clicks, claims for what its caption says, a caption written from the run, and --audit --check passing.
